title: 02 Derivatives: Visual Guide
outline: 1. Secant To Tangent | four functions with a step h you shrink from either side, drawing the secant line, the tangent line and the difference quotient's arithmetic | the derivative is the limit of the average rate of change, so the secant slope becomes the tangent slope — and at a corner the one-sided limits disagree and no derivative exists

2. Which Rule Applies | five expressions run through the power, product and quotient rules, each compared with the tempting shortcut and with a numerical derivative that knows no rules | the product rule keeps terms built from the original functions and the quotient rule is not top-over-bottom differentiated separately, and setting the derivative to zero finds the horizontal tangents

3. Trig Derivative Cycle | sin and cos with their derivative curve and a live tangent, plus an order dial showing which of the four faces the n-th derivative of sin(x) wears | sine differentiates to cosine and cosine to minus sine, so higher-order derivatives repeat with period four and only n mod 4 matters — the 100th derivative of sin is sin, the 102nd is -sin

4. Chain Implicit Rates | one rule in three modes: four compositions checked numerically, a point dragged round x^2 + y^2 = 25 with its tangent, and a circle whose radius grows at a chosen rate | the chain rule multiplies the outer derivative evaluated at the inner function by the inner derivative, which is also what makes implicit differentiation and related rates work — and in related rates the numbers go in only after differentiating

5. Tangent Line Zoom | three functions sharing f(2) = 5 and f'(2) = 3 but differing in curvature, with the approximation error shown as a bar that shrinks by a quarter each time the step halves | the linear approximation L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a) errs by about half f''(a) times the step squared, so the second derivative alone decides whether the tangent line over- or underestimates

6. Minimize The Loss | one slider over four objectives — a rectangle's area, a cost of the form ax + b/x, square loss and log loss — with the tangent's tilt telling you which way to move | an optimum is found by setting the derivative to zero and then checking the endpoints, and in model training that same derivative supplies the direction to adjust a parameter rather than the size of the error
